title: Life beyond Earth: where living things could survive

summary.text: Nobody has yet found life anywhere but on Earth. To guess where it might be, scientists first look at the hardest places on Earth where life already lives. Tiny living things called microbes live in hot springs close to boiling, in salt lakes, and in salty water trapped inside Antarctic ice. Every one of them needs liquid water. Salt keeps water liquid far below the cold that freezes plain water, so salty water under the ice of moons like Europa is one of the best places to look.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a steaming hot spring ringed with orange and green microbe mats, on the right a cracked white ice sheet with dark salty water below, and above both a starry sky with Jupiter's icy moon Europa.

intro.hook: Lay a thread across an ice cube. Lift the thread, and the ice stays behind. Now sprinkle a pinch of salt on the ice and wait one minute. Lift again, and the ice cube comes up hanging on the thread. What did the salt do to the ice?
intro.text: Salt makes ice melt, even in the cold, and that small trick matters a great deal for life. Every living thing needs liquid water. In this unit you find out which tiny living things survive in boiling water, in ice and in salt. You test, in your own freezer, how cold salty water can get before it freezes. Then you use what you found to ask the big question: could there be life on other worlds, and where should we look?
intro.art: A child's hand lifting an ice cube out of a steel bowl by a cotton thread, with a few grains of salt on the ice.

outcomes: I can say what every living thing needs: liquid water, a supply of energy, and the chemicals their body is made of.
I can explain, using my freezer test, why very salty water stays liquid in cold that freezes plain water.
I can name tiny living things that live in near-boiling water, in ice and in very salty water, and say how their bodies deal with each problem.
I can say what an extremophile is, and give one example.
I can name three places in our solar system where scientists look for life, Mars, Europa and Enceladus, and say why each one is chosen.
I can tell how Thomas Brock found bacteria living in hot springs, and what wrong idea his discovery ended.
I can say what scientists know and do not know about aliens, and give the reasons on two sides.

terms.meaning: A living thing too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria are microbes.
terms.example: The bacteria that turn milk into curd are microbes. A spoon of curd holds many millions of them.
terms.art: A spoon of curd with a round zoom bubble showing tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: Something that flows and takes the shape of its container, like water or oil. Water can also be solid ice or a gas called water vapour.
terms.example: Water in a tumbler is a liquid. Put it in the freezer and it becomes solid ice.
terms.art: Three steel tumblers: one with ice cubes, one with water, one with steam rising.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid turns into a solid. Plain water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Ice cubes form in the freezer because it is colder than 0 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A thermometer with a blue mark at 0 degrees and an ice cube beside it.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid bubbles and turns into gas all through. Plain water boils at about 100 degrees Celsius near the sea.
terms.example: Water for tea boils at about 100 degrees Celsius in Chennai, which is by the sea.
terms.art: A steel vessel of water bubbling on a stove, with a thermometer reading 100.

terms.meaning: Colder than the temperature at which plain water freezes. Minus 10 degrees means 10 degrees colder than 0.
terms.example: A big home freezer is often about minus 18 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A thermometer with numbers going down past 0 to minus 20, and a frosty freezer door beside it.

terms.example: Mango pickle sits in brine. Very salty water is also found in salt pans by the sea.
terms.art: A glass jar of lime pickle pieces sitting in cloudy salty water.

terms.meaning: A living thing that lives in a place most life could not survive, such as near-boiling water, ice, very salty water or strong acid. The word means 'lover of extremes'.
terms.example: Thermus aquaticus is a bacterium who lives in hot springs at about 70 degrees Celsius.
terms.art: A row of four small panels: a steaming spring, an ice sheet, a pink salt lake and a dark sea vent, each with tiny microbes drawn large.

terms.meaning: A place where water heated deep underground comes up out of the ground.
terms.example: Yellowstone, a park in the United States, has hundreds of hot springs. India has hot springs too, such as at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh.
terms.art: A steaming pool of blue water in rocky ground with orange edges.

terms.meaning: Ice that forms when sea water freezes. As it freezes, most of the salt is pushed out into tiny channels of brine inside the ice.
terms.example: The sea around Antarctica freezes into sea ice every winter.
terms.art: A block of sea ice cut open, showing thin dark channels running through it, with a zoom bubble of microbes inside one channel.

terms.meaning: A tiny animal, about half a millimetre long, with eight stubby legs. Tardigrades are also called water bears. They live in damp moss, soil and water.
terms.example: A tardigrade can dry out into a tiny ball and come back to life when water returns.
terms.art: A plump, eight-legged tardigrade drawn large, walking on a green moss leaf.

terms.meaning: A planet is a big round world that goes round a star. A moon is a world that goes round a planet.
terms.example: Earth and Mars are planets that go round the Sun. Europa is a moon that goes round Jupiter.
terms.art: The Sun on the left, Earth and Mars on their paths, and Jupiter with small Europa going round it.

terms.meaning: One of Jupiter's moons. Europa is covered in ice, and scientists have strong evidence of a deep salty ocean under the ice.
terms.example: NASA's Europa Clipper spacecraft was launched in 2024 to study Europa.
terms.art: A white moon criss-crossed with brown cracks, cut open to show a dark ocean under the ice.

terms.meaning: A small icy moon of Saturn. Jets of water and ice spray out of cracks near Enceladus's south pole, from an ocean under the ice.
terms.example: The Cassini spacecraft flew through the jets and found salt in them.
terms.art: A small white moon with tall feathery jets spraying out of its bottom, and Saturn's rings behind.

terms.meaning: Any life that began somewhere other than Earth. It could be as small as a microbe.
terms.example: If scientists found living microbes in Europa's ocean, that would be alien life.
terms.art: A drop of water under a microscope, with a question mark over a tiny unknown cell.

terms.meaning: The science that asks how life began, where else it could live, and how we could find it.
terms.example: An astrobiologist might study microbes in an Antarctic lake to learn where to look on Mars.
terms.art: A woman scientist in a thick coat taking a water sample through a hole in ice, with a planet drawn in the sky above.

explanations.definition: Every living thing found so far needs three things: liquid water, a supply of energy, and the chemicals their body is built from.
explanations.description: You need water, food and air. A tree needs water, sunlight and air. A microbe needs much less, but every living thing found so far needs liquid water. Inside every cell, the chemicals of life move about and join up in water. Ice is too stiff for that, and steam floats away. Living things also need energy. Plants take it from sunlight. Animals take it from food. Some microbes take it from chemicals in rocks, with no sunlight at all. Last, they need the chemicals to build their bodies, mostly carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. So when scientists hunt for life on other worlds, they look first for liquid water.
examples: A dry seed does almost nothing until you give them water. Then they swell and sprout.
Curd bacteria work in warm milk, which is mostly water.
Microbes deep in the sea, near hot vents, take their energy from chemicals in the vent water, not from sunlight.
explanations.art: Three circles joined like a Venn diagram: a water drop, a Sun with a small rock beside it for energy, and a bundle of building blocks, with a small living cell in the middle.
explanations.context: This card is about the three things every living thing needs, and why liquid water comes first.

explanations.concept: Salt keeps water liquid in deep cold
explanations.definition: Dissolving salt in water lowers its freezing point. The more salt, the colder it must get before ice forms. Very salty water stays liquid down to about minus 21 degrees Celsius.
explanations.description: When water freezes, its tiny particles line up and hold on to each other in a neat pattern. Salt particles mixed in get in the way. So salty water must get colder before the water particles can line up. Sea water, which is a little salty, freezes at about minus 2 degrees. Water with as much salt as it can hold stays liquid until about minus 21 degrees. A home freezer is usually between about minus 6 and minus 18 degrees, so very salty water in it stays liquid. This is why salt is spread on icy roads in cold countries, and why your salted ice cube melted.
examples: In cold countries, trucks spread salt on roads so ice melts and cars do not skid.
Sea water around Antarctica stays liquid at about minus 2 degrees, colder than a plain ice cube.
In the freezer test, the cup with six spoons of salt was still liquid after a whole night.
explanations.art: Two zoom circles: on the left, water particles locked in a neat pattern as ice; on the right, water particles with salt particles scattered among them, still moving freely.
explanations.context: Remember the freezer test, where plain water froze and very salty water did not? This card explains why.

explanations.concept: Life in water close to boiling
explanations.definition: Some microbes live in hot springs and deep-sea vents at 70 degrees Celsius and more. A few live above 100 degrees, in deep sea water that cannot boil because of the great weight of water above it.
explanations.description: Heat is a problem for most living things. Heat breaks the working parts inside a cell, the way heat sets runny egg white into solid white. Microbes who live in hot springs have working parts that are built to hold their shape in heat. One of them, a bacterium called Thermus aquaticus, lives best at about 70 degrees. Their working parts are so heat-proof that one of them is now used in laboratories to copy DNA, the instructions inside cells. Other microbes live deep in the sea beside hot vents in the sea floor. The water there can be hotter than 100 degrees without boiling, because so much water presses down on it. Some of these microbes keep growing above 110 degrees.
examples: Thermus aquaticus was found in a hot spring in Yellowstone, in the United States, in 1966.
The bright orange and yellow rings around some hot springs are thick mats of heat-loving microbes.
Tests that look for the virus that causes COVID use a heat-proof chemical first found in Thermus aquaticus.
explanations.art: A steaming hot spring seen from above, with a deep blue centre and rings of yellow, orange and brown at the edges, and a zoom bubble of rod-shaped bacteria.
explanations.context: This card is about microbes who live in water almost hot enough to boil, and how their bodies deal with the heat.

explanations.definition: Microbes live in the thin channels of salty water inside sea ice, and in salty lakes sealed under ice in Antarctica, at temperatures well below zero.
explanations.description: Cold is a different problem. It slows everything down, and ice crystals can grow and burst a cell. But ice is not always solid all the way through. When sea water freezes, most of the salt is pushed out of the ice into thin channels of brine. The brine stays liquid, and bacteria and tiny algae live in those channels. Some of them make substances that stop ice crystals growing inside them. In Antarctica, Lake Vida lies under about 20 metres of ice. Its water is about six times saltier than the sea and about minus 13 degrees. In 2012, a team led by Alison Murray, an American scientist, reported bacteria living in it.
examples: Tiny algae in Antarctic sea ice can colour the bottom of the ice brown.
Lake Vida in Antarctica has bacteria living in brine at about minus 13 degrees.
In the sea ice test, the leftover water under the ice tasted saltier than the water you started with, because freezing pushed the salt out.
explanations.art: A cut-away of Lake Vida: a thick white ice lid, dark salty water beneath, and a scientist in a red coat drilling through the top.
explanations.context: This card is about microbes who live inside ice and under ice, far colder than your freezer's ice tray.

explanations.concept: Life in salt and in dry places
explanations.definition: Salt-loving microbes live in water so salty that it would pull the water out of most cells. Tardigrades survive drying out by curling into a dry ball and waiting for water.
explanations.description: Very salty water is a problem because salt pulls water out of living cells. Salted cucumber slices go limp for this reason. Salt-loving microbes fill their own cells with salts too, so the water stays inside them. Many of them are pink or red. In 2020, Lonar Lake in Maharashtra turned pink. The lake had become very salty in the hot, dry weather, and scientists in Pune found it was full of pink salt-loving microbes called haloarchaea. Drying out is another problem. A tardigrade lives in damp moss, which dries up in the hot months. So the tardigrade pulls in their head and legs and dries into a tiny ball. They can wait like this for years. When water comes back, they unroll and walk again.
examples: Lonar Lake in Maharashtra, which fills a crater made by a falling space rock, turned pink in 2020 because of salt-loving microbes.
Salt pans by the sea can turn pink when salt-loving microbes grow in them.
In 2007, dried tardigrades were sent into space on the outside of a spacecraft. Some survived and later laid eggs.
explanations.art: A round crater lake with pink water and a green rim of trees, and beside it a tardigrade curled into a dry ball on a dry moss leaf.
explanations.context: This card is about life in very salty water, and a tiny animal who survives drying out.

explanations.concept: Where in our solar system scientists look for life
explanations.definition: Scientists look where there is, or once was, liquid water: Mars, Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus.
explanations.description: Mars is cold and dry today, with thin air, and its water is mostly frozen. But dried-up river beds and lake beds show that Mars once had liquid water on the surface. NASA's Perseverance rover has been collecting rock samples from an old lake bed called Jezero crater, in case they hold signs of past microbes. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, is covered in ice. Strong evidence shows a deep salty ocean under that ice, with more water than all of Earth's oceans. Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn, sprays jets of water and ice into space from an ocean under its ice. The Cassini spacecraft flew through the jets and found salt and other chemicals that living things use. Nobody yet knows if anything lives in any of these places.
examples: Perseverance landed on Mars in 2021, in an old lake bed, and has been collecting rocks there.
Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, is due to reach Jupiter in 2030.
Cassini studied Saturn and its moons from 2004 to 2017.
explanations.art: Three worlds side by side: rusty red Mars with a dry river valley, white cracked Europa with a cut-away ocean, and small Enceladus spraying jets.
explanations.context: This card is about the three places in our solar system that scientists think are the best bets for life, and why.

explanations.description: Nobody has found life beyond Earth, and nobody has shown there is none. The Milky Way, our galaxy, has more than 100 billion stars, and most stars probably have planets going round them. Some of those planets are at the right distance from their star for liquid water. That makes many scientists think life is likely somewhere. Others point out that life on Earth needed a long chain of lucky events, and complex life, like animals, took billions of years to appear. So microbes might be common, but animals and people rare. A third question is why, if life is common, nobody has heard from anyone. This is called the Fermi question, after Enrico Fermi, an Italian physicist who asked it in 1950.
examples: Since 1995, astronomers have found more than 5,000 planets going round other stars.
In 2020, a team led by Jane Greaves, a British astronomer, reported a gas in the clouds of Venus that can come from microbes. Other scientists later questioned the result, and the argument goes on.
Any alien life we find first will most likely be microbes, because microbes are the most common life on Earth.

perspectives.explanation: There are so many stars and planets that life has very likely started on some of them. Earth's microbes show that life can survive in hard places.

perspectives.who: Peter Ward and Donald Brownlee, American scientists, in their book Rare Earth (2000)
perspectives.explanation: Microbes may be common, but complex life like animals needs many conditions at once, so it may be very rare in the galaxy.

perspectives.who: Scientists who stress what we do not know
perspectives.explanation: We have only one example of life, Earth's, so we cannot yet say whether life is common or rare. We have to look.

explanations.art: A child on a flat's balcony at night looking up at a sky full of stars, with tiny planets drawn round a few of them.
explanations.context: This card is about the big question of whether aliens exist, and why scientists disagree about it.

explanations.definition: Scientists search for life in three ways: by sending spacecraft to look closely, by studying the air of faraway planets with telescopes, and by listening for signals.
explanations.description: Rovers on Mars drill into rocks and test them for the chemicals living things leave behind. Spacecraft like Europa Clipper fly past moons and measure what their ice and jets are made of. For planets round other stars, which are far too far to visit, telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope study the starlight that passes through a planet's air. Each gas takes away its own colours from the light, so scientists can tell which gases are there. Some gases, like oxygen on Earth, are made mostly by living things. Other scientists, such as the American astronomer Jill Tarter, have spent years listening with radio telescopes for signals sent on purpose by someone.
examples: Earth's air has lots of oxygen because plants and tiny algae keep making it.
Spacecraft going to Mars are cleaned very carefully, so that they do not carry Earth microbes there by mistake.
The Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977, each carry a golden record of sounds and pictures from Earth.
explanations.art: A rover drilling into red rock, a spacecraft flying through jets from an icy moon, and a big radio dish pointing at the stars.
explanations.context: This card is about how scientists actually look for life on other worlds.

agreed.text: Every living thing found so far needs liquid water.
agreed.evidence: No living thing has been found growing without it. Microbes in ice live in the liquid brine between the crystals, not in the solid ice.

agreed.text: Some microbes live in water hotter than 100 degrees Celsius, and some live in brine below minus 10 degrees.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have grown microbes from deep-sea vents in the laboratory at over 110 degrees, and found active bacteria in Lake Vida's brine at about minus 13 degrees.

agreed.text: Salt lowers the freezing point of water.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it in a home freezer. Very salty water stays liquid at minus 18 degrees, while plain water freezes at 0.

agreed.text: Mars once had liquid water on its surface.
agreed.evidence: Spacecraft have photographed dried river valleys and lake beds on Mars, and rovers have found rocks that only form in water.

agreed.text: No life has yet been found anywhere except Earth.
agreed.evidence: Every claim so far has had another explanation that most scientists find more likely.

challenging.claim: Mars is criss-crossed by canals built by Martians.
challenging.who: Percival Lowell, an American astronomer, in books from 1895 to 1908
challenging.for: Through small telescopes, some astronomers saw dark straight lines on Mars. An Italian astronomer, Giovanni Schiaparelli, had called them 'canali', which means channels.
challenging.against: In 1965, the Mariner 4 spacecraft flew past Mars and sent back close pictures. They showed craters and dry ground, and no canals. The lines had been a trick of the eye at the edge of what the telescopes could show.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that people on Mars had built canals.

challenging.claim: A meteorite from Mars, found in Antarctica, holds tiny fossils of Martian microbes.
challenging.who: David McKay and his team at NASA, in 1996
challenging.for: The rock, called ALH84001, had tiny worm-like shapes and chemicals that microbes on Earth can make.
challenging.against: Other scientists showed that the same shapes and chemicals can form without life. Most scientists today are not convinced.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous rock from Mars and an argument over what is inside it.

challenging.claim: A gas in the clouds of Venus could be a sign of living microbes.
challenging.who: A team led by Jane Greaves, a British astronomer, in 2020
challenging.for: The team reported phosphine, a gas that on Earth is mostly made by living things, high in Venus's clouds, where it is not too hot.
challenging.against: Other teams looked again and found much less phosphine, or none. Some think the signal came from a different gas, or from how the data was handled.
challenging.context: This card is about a recent argument over a possible sign of life on Venus.

challenging.claim: Life on Earth started from microbes that came here on space rocks.
challenging.who: An old idea called panspermia, argued by Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish scientist, in 1903, and by others since
challenging.for: Tardigrades and some microbes can survive in space for a while. Rocks really do travel between Mars and Earth, knocked off by big impacts.
challenging.against: There is no evidence that any Earth life came from space. And the idea only moves the question: where did that life begin?
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that life on Earth came from somewhere else.

challenging.who: What most people, and most scientists, thought before 1977
challenging.for: Plants need sunlight, and animals eat plants or eat animals that ate plants.
challenging.against: In 1977, scientists in the submarine Alvin found crabs, clams and tube worms by hot vents on the dark sea floor. Their food chain starts with microbes who take energy from chemicals in the vent water.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that all life needs sunlight, and the dark sea floor that proved it wrong.

big_questions.q: If we found microbes on Europa, would they be aliens, or our relatives?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether life could have travelled between worlds on rocks, or started again on its own.

big_questions.q: A microbe from a hot spring cannot grow at your body's warmth, and you could not survive in the spring. So which of you lives in an 'extreme' place?
big_questions.hint: Think about who decides what is normal. Is 37 degrees normal for everyone?

big_questions.q: Why does life need liquid water, and not ice or steam?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens inside a cell. Things must move and meet each other.

big_questions.q: If the galaxy is full of life, why has nobody heard from anyone?
big_questions.hint: Think about how far apart the stars are, and how short a time people have been listening.

big_questions.q: Would we know alien life if we saw it?
big_questions.hint: Think about the signs of life you know. Would a living thing that does not use water still be alive?

big_questions.q: Could life be made of something other than carbon, or live in a liquid other than water?
big_questions.hint: Saturn's moon Titan has lakes of liquid methane, not water. Scientists argue about whether anything could live there.

story.title: Sea Ice in a Chennai Freezer
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: sea water freezes more slowly than tap water, freezing pushes salt out of the ice, microbes live in the brine inside sea ice, and Lake Vida and Europa are real.
text: On Sunday evening, Kavya and her little brother Arjun came home from Marina Beach with sandy feet and a bottle of sea water. Kavya was nine. Arjun was six, and the bottle had been his idea.
"I am going to make sea ice," Arjun said. "Like at the South Pole. Then I will have penguin ice cubes."

Their mother laughed and found him an empty ice tray. Kavya filled the other half of the tray with tap water, because she wanted to see if sea ice looked any different. They pushed the tray into the freezer, next to a packet of frozen peas, and went to wash the sand off their feet.

After dinner, Arjun ran to check. He pulled out the tray and frowned. The tap-water cubes were hard and white. But the sea-water cubes were soft. When he pressed one with his finger, it squished like wet sugar, and salty water ran out of it.
"It's broken," he said. "The sea doesn't want to be ice."

Kavya pressed one too. There were little crystals of ice in it, but there was liquid all round them. "Maybe it just needs more time," she said. "The sea is salty. Maybe salt makes water slower to freeze."
"Ask Lakshmi Chithi," said their mother. "She will know."

Lakshmi Chithi was their mother's younger sister. She studied microbes, tiny living things too small to see, in a laboratory in Hyderabad. Kavya called her on the phone and turned on the video, and held the soft sea-ice tray up to the camera.

"You have made real sea ice," said Lakshmi Chithi, and she looked delighted. "Kavya, you are right about the salt. Plain water freezes at zero degrees. Salty water has to get colder before it freezes. The more salt there is, the colder it has to get."
"But why is it so wet inside?" asked Kavya.

"Because when sea water freezes, the ice pushes the salt out," said Lakshmi Chithi. "The ice crystals are made almost only of water. The salt gets squeezed into the water left between them. That leftover water gets saltier and saltier, so it stays liquid even when it is very cold. Arjun, lick one of the hard bits of ice, and then a drop of the runny water."
Arjun licked a crystal. Then he licked a drop of the liquid and screwed up his face. "The water is much saltier!" he said.

"Exactly," said Lakshmi Chithi. "The real sea ice around Antarctica is like that. It is full of thin channels of very salty water that never freeze. And here is my favourite part. Those channels are full of life. Bacteria and tiny algae live in them, in the dark and the cold, in water below zero."
Kavya stared at the tray. "Things live inside ice?"

"Inside the liquid in the ice," said Lakshmi Chithi. "Every living thing needs liquid water. Not ice, not steam. Liquid. Inside a cell, all the chemicals of life have to move about and meet each other, and they can only do that in liquid water. So wherever there is liquid water, scientists go looking for life. And they keep finding it. In Antarctica there is a lake called Lake Vida, sealed under ice as thick as a six-storey building is tall. The water in it is six times saltier than the sea, and colder than your freezer's ice tray. In 2012, a team led by a scientist called Alison Murray found bacteria living in that water."
Arjun was thinking hard. "Are there penguins in it?"

"No penguins," said Lakshmi Chithi, smiling. "Just microbes. But here is a bigger question. Far away, going round the planet Jupiter, there is a moon called Europa. Europa is covered in ice, kilometres thick. Under the ice, scientists are fairly sure there is a huge ocean of salty water. It is so far from the Sun that it should be frozen solid. But the salt, and heat from inside the moon, may keep it liquid."
"So there could be microbes in it," said Kavya slowly. "Like in Lake Vida."

"There could be," said Lakshmi Chithi. "Nobody knows yet. A spacecraft called Europa Clipper is on its way there now, to find out what the ice and the water are made of. Maybe when you are grown up, you will know the answer."

After the call, Kavya took a clean katori from the kitchen. She filled it with water, and stirred in salt, spoon after spoon, until no more would dissolve. She put it in the freezer, right at the back where it was coldest.
"What are you doing?" asked Arjun.
"Making a tiny Europa," said Kavya. "Let's see if it freezes by morning."

In the morning, the tap-water cubes were hard. The sea-water cubes had frozen at last. But Kavya's katori of very salty water was still liquid. When she tilted it, it moved like water, though the steel was so cold it stuck to her fingers for a moment.
Arjun put his face close to it. "Hello," he whispered to the water. "Is anybody in there?"
story.epiphany: For the parent: salt lowers the freezing point of water. Sea water freezes at about minus 2 degrees, so it froze more slowly than tap water. Very salty water stays liquid down to about minus 21 degrees, which is colder than home freezers, so Kavya's katori never froze. As sea water freezes, the ice crystals push the salt out into the leftover water, which is why the runny part tasted saltier. Microbes really do live in those brine channels in sea ice, and in Lake Vida's brine. Every living thing needs liquid water, so salty water under ice, on Earth or on Europa, is a place where life is possible.
ask: Why were the sea-water cubes still soft when the tap-water cubes were hard?
Why did the runny water taste saltier than the ice crystals?
Why do scientists look for life wherever there is liquid water?
Kavya's katori of very salty water did not freeze. What does that tell you about Europa's ocean?
Arjun asked the water, 'Is anybody in there?' What would you need to do to find out?

games.title: Could Life Live There? A card game of worlds and needs
games.context: This is a card game. You turn over a place card, such as a hot spring, an Antarctic lake or Mars, and decide whether a living thing could live there. You score by giving the right reason.

printables.title: 16 place cards to cut out
items: A hot spring in Yellowstone, 70 degrees, liquid water, chemicals in the water. (Yes: Thermus aquaticus lives here)
A deep-sea vent, 110 degrees, liquid water under great pressure, no sunlight. (Yes: some microbes grow here)
Lake Vida in Antarctica, minus 13 degrees, very salty liquid water under ice. (Yes: bacteria live here)
Antarctic sea ice, minus 5 degrees, thin channels of salty liquid water. (Yes: bacteria and algae live in the channels)
Lonar Lake in Maharashtra in a dry year, very salty water. (Yes: pink salt-loving microbes)
Damp moss on a wall in Bengaluru. (Yes: tardigrades)
A pot of curd at room temperature. (Yes: curd bacteria)
The inside of your mouth. (Yes: hundreds of kinds of bacteria)
A block of plain ice at minus 30 degrees, no liquid at all. (Very unlikely: there is no liquid water. Some microbes can wait frozen, but they cannot grow.)
Boiling water in a pressure cooker for 20 minutes. (No: this kills nearly all living things. That is why we cook food.)
The surface of the Moon, no air, no liquid water. (No life found: no liquid water)
The surface of Mars today, cold and dry. (Unknown: no life found, but Mars once had lakes)
Under the rocks of Mars, where ice may melt. (Unknown: scientists want to look)
Europa's ocean under the ice. (Unknown: liquid salty water, so it is one of the best places to look)
Enceladus's ocean, which sprays jets into space. (Unknown: salty water and chemicals life uses)
The surface of Venus, about 460 degrees. (No: far too hot for liquid water)

printables.title: 3 answer cards for each player
items: YES, life lives here
NO, life could not grow here
UNKNOWN, nobody knows yet

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Player name
Right answer (1 point)
Right reason (1 more point)

rules: Shuffle the 16 place cards and put them face down. Each player holds the three answer cards: YES, NO and UNKNOWN.
One player turns over the top place card and reads it aloud, without reading the answer in brackets.
Everyone puts down one answer card face down at the same time. Then all turn them over.
The reader reads the answer in brackets. A right answer scores 1 point.
Each player with the right answer then gives a reason. A reason that uses liquid water, energy or a real creature scores 1 more point.
Take turns to be the reader. When all 16 cards are done, the most points wins.
Playing alone: sort the cards into three piles, then check the answers. Try to beat your score next time.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Give each player a YES, a NO and an UNKNOWN card. 3. Shuffle the place cards.
flow.say: Each card is a place. Some have life, some do not, and for some nobody knows yet. You must decide which, and say why.
flow.kid: Each card is a place. Does life live there? Yes, no, or nobody knows?
flow.context: This is the first step of Could Life Live There?, a card game about where living things can survive.

flow.do: Play the Lake Vida card together as a practice turn.
flow.say: Practice turn. Lake Vida is in Antarctica. Its water is minus 13 degrees and very salty, under thick ice. Could anything live there?
flow.kid: Lake Vida is very cold and very salty. Can anything live there?

check.q: Lake Vida's water is minus 13 degrees and very salty, under ice. Do living things live there?
options: No, it is too cold for anything
Yes, bacteria live in the salty water
Only penguins live there
check.why: Bacteria live in Lake Vida's salty water. The salt keeps the water liquid even at minus 13 degrees, and liquid water is what life needs. Picking 'too cold' is a very common guess, but cold alone does not stop life when the water stays liquid. No penguins live under the ice.

flow.do: Play the rest of the cards. After each card, ask for a reason before giving the point.
flow.say: Before I read the answer, tell me why you chose it. Think about water, energy, and anyone you know who lives there.
flow.kid: Turn a card. Choose yes, no or unknown. Say why.
flow.parent: The best reasons mention liquid water. Watch for the plain ice card. Many children say yes because microbes live in ice, but those microbes live in liquid brine inside the ice. A block with no liquid at all is very unlikely to have anything growing in it.

flow.do: Add up the scores. Ask which card surprised them most.
flow.say: Which place surprised you most? Why?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.think: Every YES card had liquid water. Can you find a YES card without it?

games.title: Hot, Cold, Salty, Dry: a running game
games.context: This is a moving game for a room or a corridor. Four corners stand for four hard places to live. The caller names a creature, and everyone runs to the corner where that creature lives.

printables.title: 4 corner signs
items: HOT: hot springs and deep-sea vents
COLD: ice and frozen lakes
SALTY: salt lakes and salt pans
DRY: places that dry out, like moss on a wall in summer

printables.title: 12 creature cards for the caller
items: Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium from a Yellowstone hot spring (HOT)
Microbes beside deep-sea vents, growing above 100 degrees (HOT)
The orange and yellow microbe mats round a hot spring (HOT)
Bacteria in Lake Vida, Antarctica (COLD, and SALTY too)
Algae living in the brine channels of sea ice (COLD)
Pink haloarchaea in Lonar Lake in a dry year (SALTY)
Pink microbes in a salt pan by the sea (SALTY)
A tardigrade curled into a dry ball in summer moss (DRY)
A dry seed waiting in a jar for water (DRY)
Microbes in the dry Atacama Desert in Chile (DRY)
Emperor penguins in Antarctica (COLD)
A camel in the Thar Desert (DRY)

rules: Tape the four signs in four corners of the room.
The caller reads a creature card aloud.
Everyone runs to the corner where that creature lives. If a card fits two corners, you may stand between them.
The caller asks one runner: what problem does that place give the creature, and how does the creature deal with it? A good answer earns a clap.

flow.do: 1. Tape a sign in each corner. 2. Read the four signs aloud together.
flow.say: Each corner is a hard place to live. When I name a creature, run to their corner.
flow.kid: Four corners. Hot, cold, salty, dry. Run to the right one!
flow.context: This is a running game about creatures who live in hard places.

flow.do: Read the creature cards one at a time. After each run, ask one question.
flow.say: Tardigrade in summer moss! Go! Now, what problem does summer give a tardigrade, and what do they do about it?
flow.kid: Run to the corner. What is hard there? How does the creature cope?
flow.parent: Good answers name the problem first, then the trick. For example: the moss dries out, so the tardigrade curls into a dry ball and waits for rain. Heat breaks most cells' working parts, so hot-spring microbes have heat-proof parts.

flow.do: End with Lake Vida, which fits two corners.
flow.say: Last one. Bacteria in Lake Vida. Which corner? Why could it be two?
flow.kid: Lake Vida bacteria. Which corner? Could it be two?

check.q: Why does Lake Vida fit both COLD and SALTY?
options: Its water is very cold and very salty at the same time
It is cold in winter and salty in summer
It is next to the sea
check.why: Lake Vida's water is about minus 13 degrees and six times saltier than the sea, all year. The salt is what keeps it liquid in the cold, so the two go together.

setup.caption: 1. Tape a sign in each corner.

setup.caption: 2. Hear the creature, run to their corner, then explain.

experiments.title: Salt in the Freezer: how cold can water get and stay liquid?
experiments.question: Does salt stop water freezing in a home freezer? Does more salt make a difference?
experiments.predict: We will put three cups in the freezer: plain water, water with one spoon of salt, and water with six spoons of salt. Which will freeze first? Will any of them stay liquid all night? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three cups that are the same, with the same amount of water, on the same freezer shelf, checked at the same times. Only the amount of salt changes. That way, if one freezes later, the salt is the reason.

materials.item: three small cups that are the same, such as three steel katoris or three plastic cups
tap water, half a cup (about 100 millilitres) for each cup
table salt, 7 level teaspoons in all
a teaspoon for measuring and a steel spoon for poking
three small paper labels and cello tape, or a marker
a clock or phone timer
optional: a digital kitchen thermometer, to read how cold your freezer is

experiments.safety: Do not drink the salty water. It is far too salty to be good for you. When you finish, pour it down the sink with plenty of tap water. Very cold steel can stick to wet fingers for a moment, so hold the cups with dry hands or a cloth.

schedule.what: Set up three cups in the evening, check them after 1 hour and 3 hours, and once more next morning. Then explain what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each check. Write one of these four words: liquid, thin ice on top, slushy, or frozen hard. Next morning, draw the three cups and colour the ice blue and the liquid water green.

flow.do: 1. Label the cups 0, 1 and 6. 2. Pour half a cup of tap water into each. 3. Add one level teaspoon of salt to cup 1. 4. Add six level teaspoons of salt to cup 6. 5. Stir each cup for one minute.
flow.say: We are making three kinds of water. Plain, a little salty, and very salty. Stir until the salt is mostly gone.
flow.kid: Label three cups 0, 1 and 6. Add that many spoons of salt. Stir.
flow.parent: The six-spoon cup holds almost as much salt as water can take, so a little may stay at the bottom. That is fine. Level spoons matter, so scrape each one flat with the back of a knife.
flow.context: This is the first step of the freezer test. You make plain water, a little salty water, and very salty water, then see which freeze.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess what each cup will look like in 1 hour, in 3 hours and next morning. 2. Ask for a reason. 3. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Which cup will freeze first? Will any of them stay liquid all night? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which cup will freeze first? Will any stay liquid? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the salty cups will be different?
good: The sea is salty and it does not freeze at home.
Salt melted the ice cube with the thread.
Salt gets in the way of the water turning to ice.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Any reason your child gives is useful, because it shows what they think now.

flow.do: Put the three cups side by side on the same shelf of the freezer. Note the time.
flow.say: Same shelf, side by side, so they all get the same cold. Now we wait one hour.
flow.kid: Put all three cups on one shelf. Side by side. Wait one hour.
flow.parent: If you have a digital thermometer, put its tip in the freezer too, and read the temperature later. A big double-door fridge is often about minus 18 degrees. The small freezer box of a single-door fridge is usually warmer, around minus 6 to minus 12 degrees.

flow.do: 1. Take the cups out one at a time. 2. Tap the top with the steel spoon. 3. Tilt the cup gently. 4. Write liquid, thin ice on top, slushy or frozen hard. 5. Put each cup straight back.
flow.say: Tap the top. Does the spoon go through? Tilt it gently. Does it move like water?
flow.kid: Tap each cup with a spoon. Tilt it. Liquid, slushy, or hard?
flow.parent: After an hour, the plain cup usually has ice on top and round the edges. The salty cups are usually still liquid. Work quickly so the cups do not warm up.

flow.do: Check all three cups again in the same way and write what you see.
flow.say: Two more hours have passed. Which cups have changed?
flow.kid: Check again. Which cups have changed?
flow.parent: By now the plain cup is usually frozen hard. The one-spoon cup may be slushy, with ice crystals in liquid. The six-spoon cup should still be liquid.

flow.do: 1. Check all three cups one last time. 2. Tilt the six-spoon cup over the sink. 3. Let your child hold it with a cloth and feel how cold it is.
flow.say: This cup has been in the freezer all night. Feel how cold the cup is. Is the water inside frozen?
flow.kid: Check the cups. Tilt the very salty one. Is it still liquid? Feel how cold it is.
flow.parent: The plain cup and the one-spoon cup will be frozen, though the one-spoon ice is often softer. The six-spoon cup will still pour, even though it is as cold as the freezer. A few salt crystals may sit at the bottom. If your freezer is unusually cold and the six-spoon cup has some ice crystals, it will still be much softer than the others, and that still answers the question.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: salt stops water freezing, and more salt stops it more. What I saw: the plain water froze first, the one-spoon water froze later and softer, and the six-spoon water was still liquid next morning. Why: the salt gets in the way of the water turning into ice, so salty water has to get much colder before it freezes. Now tell them about Lake Vida, a salty lake under Antarctic ice at about minus 13 degrees, where bacteria live.

check.q: The six-spoon cup stayed liquid all night in the freezer. What does this show?
options: The freezer was broken
Very salty water stays liquid in cold that freezes plain water
Salt makes water warm
check.why: The plain cup froze hard on the same shelf, so the freezer was working. The salty water was just as cold, as you felt through the cup. It stayed liquid because salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes. Picking 'salt makes water warm' is a natural guess, but the cup felt icy cold.

experiments.context: In this experiment you put plain, a little salty and very salty water in your freezer, and check which ones freeze. It shows how salt keeps water liquid in the cold, which matters for life in ice.

experiments.title: Sea Ice in a Cup: does freezing push the salt out?
experiments.question: When salty water starts to freeze, is the ice as salty as the water, or does the salt stay behind in the liquid?
experiments.predict: We will freeze salty water until it is half ice. Will the ice taste salty, or plain? Will the leftover water be more salty or less salty than at the start? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Taste the salty water before freezing, so you have something to compare. Rinse the ice quickly, so you taste the ice itself and not the salty water on its outside. Taste the ice and the leftover water one after the other, with a sip of plain water between.
results_table: Salty, a little salty, or plain?

materials.item: a plastic cup or small steel bowl
half a cup of tap water (about 100 millilitres) with half a level teaspoon of salt stirred in, about as salty as the sea
optional: two drops of food colour, to see where the colour goes
a spoon, a clean katori and a glass of plain drinking water

experiments.safety: This water is only as salty as the sea, so a small taste is safe. Use clean cups and drinking water, because you will taste it. Take only tiny sips.

schedule.what: Make sea-strength salty water and taste it. Freeze it for about 1 to 2 hours until it is half ice. Then taste the ice and the leftover water.

experiments.record: Write how salty each one tasted. If you used food colour, draw the cup and show where the colour was strongest.

flow.do: 1. Stir half a level teaspoon of salt into half a cup of drinking water. 2. Add two drops of food colour if you have it. 3. Take a tiny sip and remember how salty it is.
flow.say: This is about as salty as the sea at Marina Beach. Taste a tiny sip, and remember how salty it is.
flow.kid: Stir in the salt. Taste a tiny sip. How salty is it?
flow.context: This is the first step of Sea Ice in a Cup. You freeze sea-strength salty water and taste where the salt goes.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Then put the cup in the freezer.
flow.say: When this is half frozen, will the ice taste as salty as this? Saltier? Or plainer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will the ice taste salty or plain? Why?
flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Write down the guess and the reason.

flow.wait: Check after about 1 hour, then every 20 minutes
flow.do: 1. Check the cup. 2. When there is a layer of ice on top and liquid underneath, take it out.
flow.say: Look. Ice on top, water underneath. This is like the sea around Antarctica in winter.
flow.kid: Is there ice on top and water below? Take it out.
flow.parent: This often takes 1 to 2 hours, depending on your freezer. If it freezes solid, let it thaw on the counter until about half is liquid again. The first ice to melt is the saltiest part, so the test still works, but it is clearer when you catch it half frozen.

flow.do: 1. Lift out a piece of the ice with a spoon. 2. Rinse it under the tap for two seconds. 3. Let it melt in the clean katori, or lick it. 4. Sip plain water. 5. Taste a drop of the leftover liquid.
flow.say: First the ice. Then a sip of plain water. Then the leftover water. Which is saltier?
flow.kid: Taste the ice. Sip plain water. Taste the leftover water. Which is saltier?
flow.parent: The ice should taste much less salty than the water you started with. The leftover water should taste clearly saltier than at the start. If you used food colour, the ice is paler and the leftover water is darker. Home ice traps some salty water inside it, so the ice may not taste completely plain.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning. Then show the picture of sea ice channels.
flow.say: So where did the salt go when the water froze? What does that mean for a microbe living in sea ice?
flow.kid: Where did the salt go? Where could a microbe live in sea ice?
flow.parent: A good answer: the ice was less salty, and the leftover water was saltier, so freezing pushed the salt out of the ice. In real sea ice, this pushed-out salty water collects in thin channels. Because it is so salty, it stays liquid far below zero. Bacteria and tiny algae live in those channels.

check.q: In sea ice, where do bacteria and algae live?
options: Inside the solid ice crystals
In thin channels of very salty liquid water between the ice crystals
Only on top of the ice, in the sunshine
check.why: Freezing pushes the salt out of the ice crystals into thin channels of brine. The brine stays liquid, and living things need liquid water, so that is where they live. Picking 'inside the ice crystals' is a fair guess, but the solid ice has no liquid water for a cell to use.

experiments.context: In this experiment you freeze sea-strength salty water until it is half ice, and taste where the salt went. It shows how real sea ice makes the salty channels where microbes live.

activities.title: Lift an Ice Cube with a Thread

materials.item: two ice cubes from the freezer, on a steel plate
a cotton thread about 20 cm long
a pinch of table salt

activities.safety: None needed. Wash your hands after touching the salt and ice.

schedule.what: Try to lift an ice cube with a thread. Then add salt and try again.

activities.record: Draw the ice cube and the thread before and after the salt. Write one sentence about what the salt did.

flow.do: 1. Put an ice cube on a plate. 2. Lay the thread across the top. 3. Ask your child to lift the ice by the thread.
flow.say: Can you lift this ice cube with just this thread? Lay it across the top and try.
flow.kid: Lay the thread on the ice cube. Can you lift the ice?
flow.context: This is a quick puzzle to start the unit on life beyond Earth. You find out what salt does to ice.

flow.do: 1. Lay the thread across the ice again. 2. Sprinkle a pinch of salt over the thread. 3. Wait one minute. 4. Lift the thread slowly.
flow.say: Now I sprinkle a little salt on the ice, over the thread. We wait one minute. What do you think will happen when you lift it? Why?
flow.kid: Sprinkle salt on the thread. Wait one minute. Lift slowly. What happens?
flow.parent: The salt melts a thin layer of ice under the thread. The cold ice around it then freezes that water again, round the thread, so the thread is stuck in. If it does not work, wait a little longer, up to two minutes, and use a damp thread.

flow.do: Ask what the salt did. Ask what the child wonders.
flow.say: The salt made the ice melt for a moment. What do you notice? What do you wonder about salt and ice?
flow.kid: Salt melted the ice. What do you wonder about salt and ice?

ask.q: What do you think salt does to ice?
good: It makes it turn back into water even when cold.
It stops water from staying frozen.

flow.parent: Write down the child's questions. The freezer test answers the main one: does salt keep water liquid in the cold?

activities.context: This is a quick puzzle to start the unit. You lift an ice cube with a thread, using a pinch of salt.

activities.title: The Life Thermometer: a string from minus 20 to 120 degrees

materials.item: a long string or a strip of newspaper, about 3 metres
14 small cards or paper slips and a pen
cello tape or clothes pegs

schedule.what: Make a long thermometer on the floor and put living things and places on it at their temperatures.

activities.record: Take a photo or draw the string with the cards. Circle the part of the string where life has been found.

flow.do: 1. Lay the string along the floor of a corridor. 2. Write numbers on cards: minus 20, 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 and 120. 3. Put them along the string, evenly spaced, about 40 cm apart.
flow.say: This string is a giant thermometer. This end is minus 20 degrees, colder than a freezer. That end is 120 degrees, hotter than boiling water.
flow.kid: Lay out the string. Put the numbers in order, from minus 20 to 120.
flow.context: This is an activity where you make a long thermometer on the floor, and find where on it living things have been found.

flow.do: Read each place card aloud. Your child puts it on the string at the right number.
flow.say: Where does this go? Water freezes, 0. Your body, 37. Boiling water near the sea, 100. A hot day in many Indian cities, about 45. A big freezer, minus 18. Thermus aquaticus in a hot spring, about 70. Lake Vida bacteria, minus 13. Microbes by deep-sea vents, up to about 113.
flow.kid: Put each card on the string at its number.
flow.parent: Write each of these on a card first: plain water freezes, 0. Your body, 37. A hot day in many Indian cities, 45. Boiling water near the sea, 100. A big home freezer, minus 18. Curd bacteria work best, about 40. Thermus aquaticus, about 70. Lake Vida bacteria, minus 13. Microbes at deep-sea vents, up to about 113. Very salty water freezes, minus 21.

flow.do: Ask your child to stand where people live, then where any life has been found.
flow.say: Stand on the part of the string where you could live. Now walk to the coldest place life has been found. Now to the hottest. How much of the string is that?
flow.kid: Stand where you could live. Now walk to the coldest and hottest life.

check.q: Where on the string has life been found?
options: Only from about 0 to 40 degrees, where people are comfortable
From below minus 10 to above 110 degrees
Only below 0 degrees
check.why: Microbes have been found growing in brine at about minus 13 degrees and in deep-sea vents above 110 degrees. People are comfortable in a tiny part of that range. Picking 'only where people are comfortable' is the most common guess, because we judge from our own bodies.

activities.context: In this activity you lay a giant thermometer on the floor, and place people, food, ice and microbes on it at their temperatures.

activities.title: Design a Living Thing for Europa

materials.item: paper, pencils and colours
the three world cards below, read aloud

schedule.what: Choose Europa, Mars or Enceladus. List the problems a living thing would face there. Draw a living thing whose body solves each one.

activities.record: Draw your living thing, and label each feature with the problem it solves.

flow.do: Read the three world cards aloud. Europa: an ocean of dark, salty water under kilometres of ice, very cold, no sunlight. Mars: cold, dry, thin air, strong sunlight that burns living cells, ice under the ground. Enceladus: a small salty ocean under ice, with warm vents on the sea floor.
flow.say: Choose one world. Real scientists think tiny life might live in places like these. What would be hard about living there?
flow.kid: Choose Europa, Mars or Enceladus. What would be hard about living there?
flow.context: This is a design activity. You invent a living thing who could survive on another world, using what Earth's extremophiles do.

flow.do: Help your child list three problems their world would give a living thing.
flow.say: Let's list three problems first. For Europa: it is dark, so there is no sunlight for energy. It is very cold. And the water is salty.
flow.kid: Write three problems. Dark? Cold? Salty? Dry?
flow.parent: Keep each problem real: cold, dark, salty, dry, burning sunlight, no food. Each one has a real Earth creature who deals with it.

flow.do: Your child draws a living thing and labels a feature for each problem.
flow.say: For each problem, give your creature a way to deal with it. What does a microbe in Lake Vida do about the cold? What could your creature eat if there is no sunlight?
flow.kid: Draw your creature. Give them one trick for each problem. Label it.
flow.parent: Good features come from real extremophiles. Salt inside their cells so the salty water does not pull water out. Substances that stop ice crystals growing. Taking energy from chemicals at vents, like deep-sea microbes. Curling up dry and waiting, like a tardigrade. A microbe is just as good an answer as a big creature, and more likely.

flow.do: Ask how big the creature is, and why.
flow.say: How big is your creature? Is it more likely that life on Europa would be big or tiny? Why?
flow.kid: How big is your creature? Would life there be big or tiny?
flow.think: On Earth, microbes lived alone for billions of years before any animals. What does that suggest about the first life we find elsewhere?

activities.context: In this activity you design a living thing who could survive on Europa, Mars or Enceladus, using tricks real Earth creatures use.

activities.title: What Would an Alien Look Like? Ask Five People

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
five family members, neighbours or friends, asked in person or by phone

activities.safety: Ask only people your family knows. A grown-up makes any phone calls.

schedule.what: Ask five people what an alien would look like. Tally the answers and compare them with what scientists expect.

activities.record: Make a tally chart: big creature with a head and eyes, animal-like, plant-like, microbe, other. Then draw a bar chart.

flow.do: Your child asks each person two questions and writes the answers.
flow.say: Ask each person: if we find life on another world, what will it look like? And how big will it be?
flow.kid: Ask five people. What will alien life look like? How big?
flow.context: This is a small survey. You find out what people think aliens look like, and compare it with what scientists expect.

flow.do: Make a tally of the answers in groups.
flow.say: Let's put the answers in groups. How many said a creature with a head and eyes? How many said a microbe?
flow.kid: Tally the answers. Head and eyes? Animal? Plant? Microbe?

flow.do: Compare the results with what scientists expect.
flow.say: Most scientists expect the first alien life we find to be microbes. Why do you think so few people said that?
flow.kid: Scientists expect microbes first. Why did so few people say that?
flow.parent: Films and cartoons show aliens with heads and eyes. Scientists expect microbes because on Earth, microbes lived alone for about 3 billion years before animals appeared, and microbes still live in far more places than animals do.

check.q: Why do most scientists expect the first alien life we find to be microbes?
options: Microbes are the most common life on Earth, and lived alone here for billions of years
Microbes are easier to photograph
Big aliens would hide from us
check.why: On Earth, microbes were the only life for about 3 billion years, and they still live in the most places, including ice, salt lakes and hot springs. So life elsewhere is most likely to be microbes too. The other two answers are guesses with nothing to back them.

challenges.title: A Message for Anyone Out There
challenges.problem: Design a message on one sheet of paper that a living being from another world could understand, even though they do not know any of our languages.
constraints: It must say at least three things: where we are, what we look like, and something we know.
general: In 1974, scientists sent a radio message from the Arecibo telescope in Puerto Rico. It was a picture made of 1,679 dots, showing numbers, a person and our solar system.

The two Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977, each carry a golden record with sounds and pictures from Earth, and a drawing on the cover showing how to play it and where Earth is. The writer Ann Druyan was the creative director of the record.
Many messages use counting, because counting is the same everywhere: one dot, two dots, three dots.
creative: Draw the Sun and eight planets in a row, with Earth marked, to show where we are.
Draw a hand with five fingers next to five dots, to show how we count.
Draw a water drop, because anyone who is alive may need water too.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own message. Show it to someone in your family without explaining it. Can they work out what it says?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Talk about why words will not work.
flow.say: Someone from another world would not know Tamil, Hindi or English. What could we show them that they might understand?
flow.kid: Aliens do not know our words. What could you draw instead?
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You make a message for living beings on another world, without using any words.

flow.do: Read how the Arecibo and Voyager teams solved it.
flow.say: Real scientists have done this twice. They used counting, pictures, and a map of the planets. Why do you think counting was a good start?
flow.kid: Scientists used counting and pictures. Why would counting work?

flow.kid: Show it to someone. Don't explain. What do they think it says?
flow.think: Would a being with no eyes understand a picture? What else could you send?

challenges.title: Don't Take Earth Germs to Mars
challenges.problem: Spacecraft must not carry Earth microbes to Mars, or we might find our own microbes and think they are Martian. Build a small 'lander' and get it into a clean box without leaving any 'microbes' on it.
constraints: The 'microbes' are a pinch of turmeric powder rubbed on your hands.
You must pick up the lander and put it in a clean plastic box.
At the end, there must be no yellow marks on the lander or inside the box.
materials: a small toy or a paper cup as the lander
a clean plastic box with a lid
plastic bags, cloth, tongs, a spoon and soap
general: Real spacecraft are built in clean rooms, where the air is filtered and workers wear gowns, gloves and masks.
Parts are wiped with alcohol, and some are baked in ovens to kill microbes before launch.
The two Viking landers, which landed on Mars in 1976, were heated for many hours before launch to kill the microbes on them.
creative: Put plastic bags over your hands like gloves.
Use tongs or two spoons so your hands never touch the lander.
Wash your hands well and dry them before you start.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own clean way, try it, and check for yellow marks. Then try to do it faster without leaving any.

flow.do: 1. Rub a pinch of turmeric onto your child's hands. 2. Explain that the turmeric stands for microbes.
flow.say: Pretend this turmeric is Earth microbes. Real microbes are too small to see, so we use turmeric to see where they go.
flow.kid: The turmeric is pretend microbes. Don't let it touch the lander!
flow.context: This is an engineering challenge. You find a way to move a lander into a box without leaving pretend microbes on it, the way spacecraft are kept clean.

flow.do: Try once with bare yellow hands. Look for marks.
flow.say: First, just pick it up and put it in the box. Now look. Can you see yellow marks?
flow.kid: Pick up the lander with yellow hands. Any marks?
flow.parent: There will be yellow marks. This shows how easily microbes travel on hands. Wipe the lander and the box clean before the next try. Turmeric can stain cloth and plastic, so use an old cloth.

flow.do: Your child plans and tries a clean way, checking after each try.
flow.say: Now plan a clean way. You can use gloves, tongs or washing. Try it, then check for yellow.
flow.kid: Plan a clean way. Try it. Check for yellow. Try again.

flow.do: Talk about why this matters.
flow.say: Why do space scientists care so much about keeping spacecraft clean?
flow.kid: Why must spacecraft be so clean?

check.q: Why are spacecraft to Mars cleaned so carefully?
options: So they look shiny in photos
So Earth microbes do not travel to Mars, where we might mistake them for Martian life
So they are lighter
check.why: Earth microbes can survive hard places. If they rode to Mars on a spacecraft, a rover might later find them and we could not tell if they were Martian. They could also harm any life already there. Shiny and light are not the reasons.
