quiz.p: What does every living thing found so far need?
opts: Sunlight
Liquid water
Warm weather
quiz.why: Liquid water. Vent microbes live without sunlight, and Lake Vida bacteria live below zero, but all need liquid water. Picking sunlight is common, because plants need it.

quiz.p: In the freezer test, Lakshmi's cup of very salty water was still liquid next morning. Why?
opts: Salt lowers the freezing point of water
The salty cup was warmer
Salt water is too heavy to freeze
quiz.why: Salt gets in the way of water particles lining up into ice, so salty water must get much colder before it freezes. The cup was just as cold as the plain one.

quiz.p: Plain water freezes at 0 degrees. About when does water with as much salt as it can hold freeze?
opts: At 10 degrees
At 0 degrees too
At about minus 21 degrees
quiz.why: Very salty water stays liquid until about minus 21 degrees, colder than a home freezer.

quiz.p: Thermus aquaticus lives in hot springs at about 70 degrees. How does heat affect most other cells?
opts: Heat breaks their working parts, the way heat sets egg white
Heat makes them grow faster forever
Heat has no effect
quiz.why: Heat breaks most cells' working parts. Thermus aquaticus's working parts are built to hold their shape in heat.

quiz.p: Where do microbes live in sea ice?
opts: Inside the solid crystals
In thin channels of salty liquid water
Only on top
quiz.why: Freezing pushes salt into thin channels of brine. The brine stays liquid, and the microbes live there.

quiz.p: Salty water pulls water out of most cells. How do salt-loving microbes deal with this?
opts: They fill their cells with salts too, so water stays inside
They drink fresh water
They live only in rain
quiz.why: With salts inside as well as outside, water is not pulled out. Many salt-loving microbes are pink, like the ones that turned Lonar Lake pink in 2020.

opts: A very big animal
A living thing who lives where most life could not survive
A kind of spacecraft
quiz.why: Extremophile means 'lover of extremes', such as near-boiling water, ice or very salty water.

quiz.p: Why is Europa, a moon of Jupiter, one of the best places to look for life?
opts: It is the closest moon to Earth
It has a deep salty ocean of liquid water under its ice
It is very hot
quiz.why: Liquid water is what life needs, and Europa probably has more of it than all of Earth's oceans.

quiz.p: Why do scientists study rocks from an old lake bed on Mars?
opts: Mars once had liquid water, so microbes might have lived there long ago
Mars has many cities
The rocks are made of gold
quiz.why: Dried river and lake beds show Mars once had liquid water. Rocks from an old lake bed might hold signs of past microbes.

quiz.p: Before Thomas Brock's work in Yellowstone in the 1960s, what did many biologists think?
opts: Life could not survive in water much hotter than about 73 degrees
Hot springs were full of fish
Microbes could only live in ice
quiz.why: Brock found bacteria in springs at 70 degrees and pink threads of bacteria in water even hotter, which showed the old limit was wrong.

quiz.p: What do scientists know about aliens today?
opts: Aliens have visited Earth many times
No life has yet been found beyond Earth, and nobody knows if there is any
Scientists have proved there are no aliens
quiz.why: Every claim so far has had a better explanation. But we have searched only a few places, so the question is open.

quiz.p: Kavya says, 'The first alien life we find will probably be microbes.' Which fact supports her best?
opts: Microbes are the most common life on Earth, and lived alone here for billions of years
Microbes are pink
Films show microbes
quiz.why: On Earth, microbes came first and still live in the most places. So life elsewhere is most likely to be microbes too.

items.p: Name the three things every living thing found so far needs.
items.a: Liquid water, a supply of energy (such as sunlight, food or chemicals), and the chemicals their body is built from.
items.why: A strong answer names liquid water, not just water, because ice and steam are no use to a cell.

items.p: In the freezer test, which cup froze first?
opts: The plain water
The one-spoon cup
The six-spoon cup
items.why: Plain water freezes at 0 degrees, so it freezes first. Salt lowers the freezing point, so the salty cups must get colder.

items.p: In the freezer test, the six-spoon cup was still liquid next morning, but the plain cup was frozen hard. Both sat on the same shelf all night. Explain why.
items.a: Salt lowers the freezing point of water. The salt particles get in the way of the water particles lining up into ice. Very salty water does not freeze until about minus 21 degrees, which is colder than a home freezer.
items.why: A strong answer says the cups were equally cold, so the difference must come from the salt, and says what salt does.

items.p: The six-spoon cup stayed liquid because it was warmer than the plain cup.
items.why: False. Both cups were in the same freezer all night, and the salty cup felt icy cold. It stayed liquid because salt lowers the freezing point, not because it was warm.

items.p: Sort these places. Has life been found living there, or not?
items: a hot spring at 70 degrees
Life found
Antarctic sea ice
Life found
Lake Vida's salty water at minus 13 degrees
Life found
a very salty lake
Life found
the surface of the Moon
No life found
the surface of Venus at 460 degrees
No life found
water boiled in a pressure cooker
No life found
items.a: see items
items.why: Every place with life has liquid water. The Moon has no liquid water, Venus is far too hot, and pressure-cooking kills nearly all living things.

items.p: A living thing who lives in a place most life could not survive, such as near-boiling water, is called an ____.
items.why: Extremophile means 'lover of extremes'.

items.p: Match each living thing to the hard place they live in.
pairs: moss that dries out in summer
hot water deep in the sea, with no sunlight
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these lives where most life could not. Knowing where they live helps scientists choose where to look on other worlds.

items.p: Shreya, a girl in Class 3, says, 'Heat breaks the working parts inside most cells.' How do hot-spring microbes survive?
opts: They stay cool by swimming fast
Their working parts are built to hold their shape in heat
They only come out at night
items.why: Their working parts are heat-proof, so they keep working in hot water. Swimming does not cool them, and the spring is hot day and night.

items.p: Draw a cup of sea water that is half frozen. Show where the ice is, and where the salt has gone.
items.a: Ice on top, almost without salt. Salty leftover water underneath, with the salt drawn as dots crowded in the liquid.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the salt pushed out of the ice and into the liquid, as the taste test showed.
items.art: An empty outline of a cup.

items.p: In the Sea Ice in a Cup test, the ice tasted less salty than the water you started with. Where did the salt go?
items.a: Into the leftover water under the ice. That water tasted saltier than at the start. Freezing pushes the salt out of the ice crystals.
items.why: A strong answer uses both tastes as evidence: the ice was plainer and the leftover water saltier.

items.p: Why do scientists look for life where there is liquid water?
opts: Water looks nice in photos
Every living thing found so far needs liquid water
Water is easy to find everywhere in space
items.why: Inside every cell, the chemicals of life move and join up in liquid water. No living thing has been found growing without it.

items.p: Microbes living in sea ice live inside the solid ice crystals.
items.why: False. They live in the thin channels of liquid brine between the crystals. Solid ice has no liquid water for a cell to use.

items.p: Arjun, a boy of six, says, 'Nothing could live in Antarctica's ice. It is too cold.' What would you tell him, and what evidence would you use?
items.a: I would tell him that microbes live in the salty liquid water inside sea ice, and in Lake Vida under Antarctic ice at minus 13 degrees. My freezer test showed that salty water stays liquid far below zero, and living things need liquid water, not warmth.
items.why: A strong answer is kind, uses a real example, and uses the freezer test as evidence.

items.p: Put these in order from coldest to hottest.
items: boiling water near the sea
your body
Lake Vida's water
a hot spring with Thermus aquaticus
plain water freezing
a: a hot spring with Thermus aquaticus
items.why: Lake Vida is about minus 13, freezing is 0, your body is 37, the spring about 70, and boiling 100.

items.p: Label the picture of Europa: ice shell, salty ocean, rocky inside.
items.a: The outer white layer is the ice shell. Under it is the salty ocean. In the middle is the rocky inside.
items.why: Scientists think Europa's ocean sits between the ice shell and the rock, which is why it may hold life.
items.art: A cut-away drawing of Europa with three empty label lines pointing to the outer layer, a dark middle layer and the centre.

items.p: Meenakshi does the freezer test with a cup of sugar water as well. It freezes, but later than plain water. What does that tell her?
opts: Only salt can lower the freezing point
Other things dissolved in water lower the freezing point too
Sugar makes water colder
items.why: Anything dissolved in water gets in the way of ice forming, so it lowers the freezing point. Salt does it more strongly for each spoon than sugar.

items.p: Kavya's freezer is a small single-door fridge, at about minus 8 degrees. Her one-spoon cup stayed slushy all night. In her cousin's big fridge, at minus 18, the one-spoon cup froze. Explain both results.
items.a: One spoon of salt lowers the freezing point a few degrees below zero. At minus 8, the cup was only a little below its freezing point, so it froze slowly and stayed slushy. At minus 18, it was much colder than its freezing point, so it froze.
items.why: A strong answer compares each freezer's temperature with the salty water's freezing point.

items.p: If a home freezer were colder than minus 21 degrees, even the six-spoon cup would freeze.
items.why: True. Water with as much salt as it can hold freezes at about minus 21 degrees. Below that, even very salty water freezes. Home freezers are not usually that cold.

items.p: Sort each problem with the way a living thing deals with it.
items: working parts built to hold their shape when hot
Heat
filling their cells with salts so water stays inside
Salt
curling into a dry ball and waiting for water
Drying out
taking energy from chemicals instead of sunlight
Darkness
items.a: see items
items.why: Each hard place gives a different problem, and each extremophile has a way to deal with theirs. The problem comes first, then the trick.

items.p: Lonar Lake in Maharashtra turned pink in 2020, in very hot, dry weather. Explain how the dry weather could help pink salt-loving microbes.
items.a: In hot, dry weather, water evaporated from the lake, but the salt stayed behind. So the lake got saltier. Pink salt-loving microbes live well in very salty water, while many other microbes do not, so they grew and turned the lake pink.
items.why: A strong answer links evaporation to more salt, and more salt to the pink microbes.

items.p: A deep-sea vent can be hotter than 100 degrees, but the water does not boil. Why?
opts: The water is salty
The great weight of water above presses on it
It is dark down there
items.why: Pressure from the water above stops it boiling. Salt raises the boiling point only a little, and darkness has nothing to do with boiling.

items.p: Three people argue about where to send the next spacecraft to look for life.

views.says: Mars. It is close, rovers already work there, and it once had lakes. We could find signs of old microbes in the rocks.
Europa. It has liquid salty water right now, more than all of Earth's oceans. Life needs liquid water today, not long ago.
Enceladus. It sprays its ocean into space, so we can fly through the jets and test the water without drilling through ice.

items.ask: Which mission would you choose? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one good point that another person made.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and backs it: for example, Europa, because liquid water is what every living thing needs, as the freezer test showed salty water can stay liquid in deep cold. It then admits a fair point, such as that Enceladus's jets make sampling easier.
items.why: This is a real argument among space scientists. Each place has strengths, and the money for missions is limited.

items.p: Salty water inside sea ice is called ____.
items.why: Brine means very salty water. It stays liquid in the cold.

items.p: Put these steps of the freezer test in order.
items: Put the cups side by side in the freezer
Explain what you saw
Add 0, 1 and 6 spoons of salt
Check after 1 hour, 3 hours and next morning
Guess what will happen and why
a: Guess what will happen and why
Put the cups side by side in the freezer
Check after 1 hour, 3 hours and next morning
items.why: The guess comes before the test, so the test can show whether the guess was right.

items.p: Why did the freezer test use three cups that were the same, on the same shelf?
opts: So only the amount of salt changed
So the cups looked neat
So they would freeze faster
items.why: Keeping everything else the same is called a fair test. Then any difference must come from the salt.

items.p: Draw a tardigrade in moss in the rainy season, and the same tardigrade in summer when the moss is dry.
items.a: In the rain, a tardigrade walking on eight stubby legs in wet moss. In summer, the tardigrade curled into a small dry ball with no legs showing.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the problem, the moss drying, and the trick, curling into a dry ball until water returns.
items.art: Two empty boxes labelled 'rainy season' and 'summer'.

items.p: Thermus aquaticus cannot grow at your body's warmth, 37 degrees, because it is too cool for them. So is 37 degrees 'extreme'? Explain your answer.
items.a: For a person, 37 degrees is normal. For Thermus aquaticus, it is too cold to grow. So 'extreme' depends on who is living there. Each living thing has their own range.
items.why: A strong answer sees that 'extreme' is measured from our own bodies, and other living things have different ranges.

items.p: Mars has liquid water flowing on its surface today, like rivers on Earth.
items.why: False. Mars's water today is mostly frozen, in its polar caps and under the ground. Dried river beds show water flowed long ago.

items.p: Why do scientists think Enceladus has an ocean under its ice?
opts: Its surface is blue
It sprays jets of salty water and ice out of cracks
It is very hot
items.why: The Cassini spacecraft saw jets of water and ice coming from cracks near Enceladus's south pole, and found salt in them. Salt in the spray points to a salty ocean below.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 3, says, 'If we find life on Europa, it will be a big creature with eyes.' Do you agree? Give a reason.
items.a: Probably not. Europa's ocean is dark, so eyes may not help. On Earth, microbes are the most common life and lived alone for billions of years before animals. So the first life we find is most likely to be microbes.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fact about Earth's history or about Europa's darkness.

items.p: Match each spacecraft to what it does.
pairs: collects rocks from an old lake bed on Mars
is on its way to study Jupiter's icy moon
flew through the jets of Enceladus
showed in 1965 that Mars has no canals
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each mission added a piece to the search for life beyond Earth.

items.p: Two scientists argue about whether animals live on planets round other stars.

views.says: There are more than 100 billion stars in our galaxy, and most have planets. Life must have started on many of them, and some must have grown into animals.
On Earth, microbes lived alone for about 3 billion years before animals appeared. Animals may need a long run of lucky events. Microbes may be common but animals rare.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with more? Use a fact from this unit. Then say what evidence would change your mind.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a fact, for example the 3 billion years of microbes on Earth, and names evidence that would settle it, such as finding oxygen in a faraway planet's air, or a signal.
items.why: This is a real, open argument. Nobody knows the answer, and both use real evidence.

items.p: Plan a test: does sugar lower the freezing point as much as salt? Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would look for.
items.a: I would put two cups of the same amount of water in the freezer, one with six spoons of salt and one with six spoons of sugar. Same cups, same shelf, same times. I would check after 1 hour, 3 hours and next morning, and see which freezes first. The one that stays liquid longer lowers the freezing point more.
items.why: A strong plan changes only one thing, keeps the rest the same, and says what result would answer the question.

items.p: Europa is about five times further from the Sun than Earth, so it gets very little sunlight. Which is the most likely energy source for any life in its ocean?
opts: Sunlight shining through the thick ice
Chemicals from warm rock on the ocean floor, like at Earth's deep-sea vents
Lightning in the ocean
items.why: Very little sunlight gets through kilometres of ice. On Earth, vent microbes take energy from chemicals in the dark, so scientists think the same could happen on Europa's sea floor. There is no evidence of lightning in the ocean.

items.p: A scientist finds microbes on Mars. Another scientist says, 'They might have come from Earth on our own spacecraft.' How could the first scientist show that they are really Martian?
items.a: By showing the spacecraft was cleaned carefully, by checking that the microbes are not like any known Earth microbes, and by finding them deep in rock where a spacecraft could not have put them.
items.why: A strong answer sees why keeping spacecraft clean matters, and suggests a check that could tell Earth life from Martian life.

items.p: If no life is found on Mars, that proves there is no life anywhere beyond Earth.
items.why: False. Mars is one place. Europa, Enceladus and billions of planets round other stars would still be unexplored. Not finding something in one place does not show it is missing everywhere.

items.p: Percival Lowell saw straight lines on Mars through his telescope and said Martians had built canals. What was the best way to test his idea?
opts: Ask more people to look through the same telescope
Send a spacecraft to take close pictures
Count the lines
items.why: Mariner 4 did exactly this in 1965, and its close pictures showed craters and no canals. More people looking through the same blurry telescope could be fooled in the same way.

items.p: Thomas Brock found bacteria living in hot springs at 70 degrees and more. Before this, many biologists thought no life could live that hot. Why do you think they had believed it?
items.a: They had only looked at places where life was easy to find, and they had not tested really hot water carefully. They judged from the living things they knew.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a belief can come from not looking, not from evidence that something is impossible.

items.why: Mariner 4 flew past Mars in 1965. Thermus aquaticus was grown in 1966. Cassini found salt in the jets around 2009. Bacteria in Lake Vida were reported in 2012.

items.p: Which of these would be the strongest sign of life in a faraway planet's air?
opts: Water vapour
A lot of oxygen together with methane
Dust
items.why: On Earth, oxygen and methane react with each other, so both stay plentiful only because living things keep making them. Water vapour and dust can come from places with no life.

items.p: The science that asks where else life could live, and how we could find it, is called ____.
items.why: Astro means star, and biology is the study of life.

items.p: Some people think that if aliens exist, they must be like us. Write two reasons why life on another world might be very different from life on Earth.
items.a: Their world might be much colder, darker or saltier, so their bodies would have different ways to deal with it, like extremophiles do. And their life started separately, so it might use different chemicals, or even a liquid other than water.
items.why: A strong answer gives reasons, not just guesses, and uses what extremophiles show.

items.a: The pale top layer is the ice. The darker liquid underneath is the salty leftover water. In real sea ice, microbes live in thin channels of that salty water inside the ice.

items.p: Tardigrades are extremophiles that prefer living in very harsh places.
items.why: False. Tardigrades live in ordinary damp moss and soil. They can survive harsh conditions by drying out and waiting, but they do not live and grow there. Scientists argue about whether to call them extremophiles at all.

items.p: Why do space scientists say 'follow the water'?
opts: Water is easy to see from space
Every living thing found so far needs liquid water, so where there is liquid water, life is possible
Water is the only thing in space
items.why: Liquid water is the first thing scientists look for, because life as we know it cannot grow without it.

open_questions.q: Is there life anywhere beyond Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has found any, and we have searched only a few places closely.

open_questions.q: Is there life in Europa's ocean?
open_questions.why_open: Europa very likely has a salty ocean, but nobody has looked inside it yet. Europa Clipper will study its ice and surface from above.
Mars once had lakes and rivers. Perseverance has collected rock samples, but bringing them to Earth for testing is still being planned.

open_questions.q: What is the hottest temperature any living thing can grow at?
open_questions.why_open: The record keeps rising as new microbes are found. Scientists think the limit is somewhere around 120 to 150 degrees, but nobody knows exactly.

open_questions.q: If life is common in the galaxy, why has nobody heard from anyone?
open_questions.why_open: This is the Fermi question. There are many possible answers, such as great distances, short listening time, or that complex life is rare, and no way yet to choose between them.

open_questions.q: Could life use a liquid other than water?
open_questions.why_open: Saturn's moon Titan has lakes of liquid methane. Some scientists think life might be possible there, and others doubt it. NASA's Dragonfly mission is due to go to Titan.

maths.problem: Plain water freezes at 0 degrees. Water with as much salt as it can hold freezes at about minus 21 degrees. How many degrees colder must the very salty water get before it freezes?
maths.explain: From 0 down to minus 21 is 21 steps of one degree. On a thermometer, count down from 0 to minus 21.
maths.context: This is about the freezer test, where plain water froze and very salty water stayed liquid.
maths.why_maths: Counting below zero on a thermometer shows how much colder salty water can get and still stay liquid.

maths.problem: Bacteria in Lake Vida live at about minus 13 degrees. Some microbes at deep-sea vents grow at about 113 degrees. How many degrees apart are these two temperatures?
maths.explain: From minus 13 up to 0 is 13 degrees. From 0 up to 113 is 113 degrees. 13 + 113 = 126.
maths.context: This is about the Life Thermometer, the string on the floor from minus 20 to 120 degrees.
maths.why_maths: Splitting the jump at 0 makes it easy to add across zero, and shows how wide the range of life is.

maths.problem: One level teaspoon of salt weighs about 6 grams. In the freezer test, how many grams of salt went into the six-spoon cup? How many grams did you use in all three cups?
maths.answer: 36 grams in the six-spoon cup. 42 grams in all.
maths.explain: 6 spoons times 6 grams is 36 grams. The one-spoon cup had 6 grams and the plain cup had none. 36 + 6 + 0 = 42 grams.
maths.context: This is about the freezer test, where three cups had 0, 1 and 6 spoons of salt.
maths.why_maths: Turning spoons into grams lets someone else repeat your test exactly, even with a different spoon.

maths.problem: Lakshmi asked 10 people what alien life would look like. 6 said a creature with a head and eyes, 2 said like an animal, 1 said like a plant, and 1 said a microbe. Draw a bar chart. What fraction of people said a microbe?
maths.answer: 1 out of 10, which is one tenth.
maths.explain: Only 1 of the 10 people said a microbe. 1 out of 10 is one tenth. Most scientists would say a microbe, so the chart shows how different films and science can be.
maths.context: This is about the survey where you ask people what alien life would look like.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which answer was most common, and how far it is from what scientists expect.

roots.context: We have frozen salty water, tasted sea ice and met microbes in boiling springs and Antarctic brine. Now we ask what this tells us about life, and about our place among the worlds.

deep_truth.truth: In the freezer, your plain water froze hard, but the very salty water stayed liquid. Salt keeps water liquid in cold that freezes plain water solid. Living things need liquid water, and microbes live in salty water trapped in Antarctic ice. So the salty oceans under the ice of moons like Europa could hold life too.
deep_truth.habit: We think of icy places as dead, because cold feels deadly to us. But what life needs is liquid water, not warmth, and salt keeps water liquid far below zero.
deep_truth.evidence: In the freezer test, the six-spoon cup still poured after a night at freezer cold, while the plain cup froze hard. In Antarctica, bacteria live in Lake Vida's brine at about minus 13 degrees.

three.who_am_i: You are mostly water, and your body keeps that water liquid and warm every moment you are alive.
three.what_is_life: Life is found wherever there is liquid water and some energy, from springs near boiling to brine below zero.
three.what_is_this_world: Earth is one world with liquid water. Europa and Enceladus may be others, so Earth may not be the only home for life.

roots.thread: All life on Earth comes from one shared ancestor, and all of it needs the same thing, liquid water. From that one start came hot-spring bacteria, sea-ice algae, tardigrades, banyan trees and you. Each found their own way to live in their own place, hot or cold, salty or dry. One kind of chemistry, worked out in countless ways, has filled every corner of Earth that has liquid water.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done in a city flat. Choices made: the freezer test uses 0, 1 and 6 level teaspoons of salt in half a cup of water. Six spoons is close to as much as water can hold, which freezes only at about minus 21 degrees, colder than any home freezer, so that cup stays liquid even in a big fridge at minus 18. The one-spoon cup freezes later and softer, so there is a clear middle result. Steel katoris freeze fastest, so checks at 1 hour and 3 hours show a difference. Single-door fridges are warmer, around minus 6 to minus 12, and the steps say so. The sea-ice taste test uses sea-strength water, which is safe to taste in tiny sips, and catches the cup half frozen. If it freezes solid, partly thawing it still works. Food colour is optional and makes the result visible. The ice and thread trick is quick and reliable with a damp thread and up to two minutes. No step needs a garden, a hot spring or moss. The turmeric challenge can stain, so an old cloth is suggested. The spine is the ice and thread puzzle, the freezer test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes over two sessions with the freezer waits in between.

how_we_found_out.story: In the early 1960s, many biologists thought nothing could live in water much hotter than about 73 degrees Celsius. Thomas Brock, an American microbiologist, began studying the hot springs of Yellowstone National Park in 1965. In the water flowing out of one spring, Octopus Spring, he saw pink threads growing in water above 80 degrees. They were bacteria. In 1966, Brock and his student Hudson Freeze took water from another spring, Mushroom Spring, and grew a new bacterium from it in the laboratory. They named them Thermus aquaticus, and described them in 1969. Brock kept looking, and found bacteria in springs that were boiling, which at Yellowstone's height means about 93 degrees. The old limit had come from not looking in hot enough places. Later, scientists found microbes beside deep-sea vents growing above 110 degrees. A heat-proof chemical from Thermus aquaticus is now used in laboratories all over the world to copy DNA.
how_we_found_out.who: Thomas Brock, an American microbiologist, and his student Hudson Freeze
how_we_found_out.when: 1965 to 1969, at Yellowstone National Park in the United States
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Biologists thought no life could survive in water much hotter than about 73 degrees. Brock found bacteria growing in springs above 80 degrees, and even in boiling springs. Microbes have since been found growing above 110 degrees.
